{{Short description|none}}
In [[mathematics]], '''topology''' (from the [[Greek language|Greek]] words {{Langx|grc|[[wikt:τόπος|τόπος]]|lit=place, location|label=none}}, and {{Langx|el|λόγος|lit=study|label=none}}) is concerned with the properties of a [[mathematical object|geometric object]] that are preserved under [[Continuous function|continuous]] [[Deformation theory|deformations]], such as [[Stretch factor|stretching]], [[Twist (differential geometry)|twisting]], crumpling and bending, but not tearing or [[Quotient space (topology)|gluing]].

A [[topological space]] is a [[set (mathematics)|set]] endowed with a structure, called a ''topology'', which allows defining continuous deformation of subspaces, and, more generally, all kinds of [[continuity (mathematics)|continuity]]. [[Euclidean space]]s, and, more generally, [[metric space]]s are examples of a topological space, as any distance or metric defines a topology. The deformations that are considered in topology are [[homeomorphism]]s and [[homotopy|homotopies]]. A property that is invariant under such deformations is a [[topological property]]. Basic examples of topological properties are: the [[topological dimension|dimension]], which allows distinguishing between a [[line (geometry)|line]] and a [[surface (mathematics)|surface]]; [[compact (topology)|compactness]], which allows distinguishing between a line and a circle; [[connectedness]], which allows distinguishing a circle from two non-intersecting circles.

The ideas underlying topology go back to [[Gottfried Leibniz]], who in the 17th century envisioned the {{lang|la|geometria situs}} and {{lang|la|analysis situs}}. [[Leonhard Euler]]'s [[Seven Bridges of Königsberg]] problem and [[Euler characteristic#Polyhedra|polyhedron formula]] are arguably the field's first theorems. The term ''topology'' was introduced by [[Johann Benedict Listing]] in the 19th century, although it was not until the first decades of the 20th century that the idea of a topological space was developed.
